Recommendation of TRAI on Open Sky Policy 
*122.    SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO:†† 
SHRI RAMAMUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: 
Will the Minister of COMM UNICATIONS AND INFORMATION 
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any recommendations/suggestions have been made by TRAI 
on Open Sky Policy for DTH and VSAT Services; 
(b) if so, the details of the recommendations/suggestions made by TRAI; 
(c) whether it is a fact that the Department of Communications has rejected 
TRAI's recommendations; and 
(d) if so, the reasons for rejecting the recommendations made by TRAI? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI DAYANIDHI MARAN): (a) to (d) Astatement is laid on 
the Table of the House: 
 Statement 
(a) and (b) Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) have submitted 
various recommendations to the Government on accelerating growth of Internet 
and Broadband in the country. These recommendations include an Open Sky 
Policy permitting use of any international satellite for Very 
††The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri K. Rama 
Mohana Rao. 

RAJYA SABHA [9 Decern ber, 2004] 
Small Aperture Terminals (VSAT) and Direct-To-Home (DTH) service. The 
details of the recommendations on Open Sky Policy are given in the enclosed 
Statement. (See below). 
(c) and (d) Permitting Open Sky Policy for VSAT&DTH services has wide 
implications involving strategic, security and policy issues among others. Some 
of the concerned Ministries/Departments have reservations on the 
recommendations of TRAI on Open Sky Policy for VSAT&DTH services. The 
role of Department of Space is critical in the formulation of final policy. 
Department of Telecommunications will further pursue with the concerned 
Ministries/Departments to evolve an acceptable position. 
Statement 
Trai Recommendations On Open Sky Policy 
Recommendation No. 3.6.2.4: 
An Open Sky policy should be adopted for VSAT operators, similar to what 
is available to ISP's and broadcasters. VSAT service providers should be allowed to 
work directly with any international satellite. 
Recommendation No. 3.6.3.5: 
An Open Sky policy should be adopted for DTH operators, similar to what 
is available to ISP's and broadcasters. DTH service providers should be allowed to 
work directly with any international satellite to ensure that a full extent of video 
and broadband services can be provided to a large subscriber base. 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Sir, the hon. Minister, in his reply, says, 
"Permitting Open Sky Policy for VSAT & DTH services has wide implications 
involving strategic, security and policy issues among others". Now, the main 
concern of the Government of India is security. We know that the INSAT 
system has got certain safeguards like traffic monitoring, inspection of 
equipment and other security-related safeguards. The same safeguards are provided 
in the foreign satellites. Will the Government of India consumer the 
recommendations of TRAI? If not, let the Minister explain the reasons. 
SHRI DAYANIDHI MARAN: Sir, permitting Open Sky Policy was 
recommended by TRAI. But the Department of Telecommunication, after 
consultations with the Departments of Space, have decided not to allow it now 
because of the issues raised by the Mi nistry of Home Affairs and also the 
Departments of Space, which concern, we feel, at this moment, is 
2 

[9 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
right and fair. So, we are not allowing it now. The question 'if we allow it', does 
not arise. 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Sir, my second supplementary... 
MR. CHAIRMAN: What is the point in your second supplementary now? 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Sir, the GoM has also recommended for 
VSAT and DTH. there. The DTH services have to take the advantage of the latest 
technology. At the same time, the hon. Minister has said that there are some 
Ministries/Departments which have reservations. Which are those 
Ministries/Departments that have reservations and what are the reservations that 
they have on VSAT & DTH? 
SHRI DAYANIDHIMARAN: As far as DTH services are concerned, we are 
allowing downlinking and uplinking of broadband services. Because the 
recommendations of TRAI are for broadband alone. We are allowing uplinking 
for DTH services provided they get the necessary license. As far as DTH rules are 
concerned, the preference is for Indian satellites. The issue of security in DTH 
stands resolved.

*128. SHRI LALIT SURI: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be

renovation of Indira Gandhi Institute of Child Health (IGICH),Habiba School and

a new Parliament building in Afghanistan.

delegation from Poland, currently on a visit to our country under the

celebrations of Golden Jubilee of the establishment of diplomatic relations 
between India and Poland.

delegation and wish our distinguished guests and enjoyable and fruitful stay in

learn more about our Parliamentary system, our country and our people, and that 
their visit to this country will further strengthen the friendly bonds that exist 
between India and Poland. Through them, we convey our greetings and best 
wishes to the Parliament and the friendly people of Poland.

Statement 
Illegal Telephone Exchanges in Delhi. 
(a) Yes, Sir. One at Palam Village and other at East Patel Nagar, Delhi. 
(b) The modus operandi in both the cases unearthed in month of October, 2004 is 
that the offender has setup an illegal telephone exchange using high-tech 
equipment and this set up was receiving incoming international calls via Internet 
and was further distributing these calls using local Public Switched Telephone 
Network (PSTN)/Mobile/Wireless in Lcoal Loop (WLL) connectivity. Reliance

complaint has been filed against these exchanges. We have taken necessary actions, in the 
past, for non-adherence of DoT directions, and I can also provide the list of people and 
agencies against whom we have taken action. 
Sir, the action that our department takes is in two ways. First, we raid the premises, 
and if we find that he possesses an illegal exchange, it is seized and the culprit arrested. 
Then, we take action against the ISP license or any operator through whom the person 
is getting illegal transit into the country. 
We have a simple method of finding out who the ISP provider is. Normally, in 
the Internet service, 'Upstream' is only 10 per cent and 'Downstream' is 90 per cent. 
But in most of the cases where such illegal traffic is taking place, the upstream and 
downstream is 50 per cent; they are equally balanced. We have also given instructions to the 
ISP providers to monitor and check such abnormalities in upstream and downstream 
figures. 
Simultaneously, we also get the call records of the telephone companies which these 
persons are using to send the calls within the country. We have a simple way of finding 
this out. These calls are only outgoing calls and not incoming calls. Moreover, the pattern of 
outgoing calls is continuous, that is, the whole set up is only making outgoing calls, 24 
hours.

the culprits. We have also seized equipments, cancelled licenses, and we have charged penalties

Under the REGP, 1,86,252 projects have been financed generating 22.75 lakh 
additional employment upto 31 st March, 2004 since its inception and a sum of Rs. 
1079.47 crore has been released as margin money assistance to entrepreneurs. 
Under the Pradhan Mantri Rozgar Yojana (PMRY) of the Government, being 
implemented through the District Industries Centres (DICs) of the States/Union 
Territories (UTs) and the banks, loans are provided to the educated 
unemployed to set up self-employment ventures. Under the PMRY, the Central 
Government allocates funds for subsidy, entrepreneurial development training 
(EDT),contingencies, etc., based on the targets of generation of employment 
opportunities assigned to each State/UT. The Central funds for subsidy are 
routed through the Reserve Bank of India 
 
23

RAJYA SABHA [9 December, 2004] 
(RBI) which, in turn, passes them on to the implementing banks for crediting the 
amounts to the loan accounts of each beneficiary. Under this Yojana, projects with 
investment upto Rs. 1 lakh in the business sector and upto Rs. 2 lakh in other 
sectors are eligible for assistance. The subsidy amount is 15 per cent of project cost 
and subject to a ceiling of Rs. 7,500/-.EIigible persons can join together in a 
partnership to get assistance for projects with investment upto Rs. 10 lakh. The 
margin money contribution of the beneficiary varies from 5 per cent to 16.25 per 
cent to 16.25 per cent of the project cost, so as to make sum of the Government 
subsidy and beneficiary's own contribution to margin money equal to 20 per cent 
of the project cost. Since the inceptio n of the PMRY, 29.98 lakh employment 
opportunities are estimated to have been created and a sum of Rs. 1382 crore has 
been released as subsidy to the unemployed beneficiaries till 31 March 2004. 
The Central Government provides assistance under the REGP and PMRY 
for setting up new units/self-employment ventures. Existing units/ self-
employment ventures, which were set up with credit from banks and margin 
money assistance from the Government but have now become sick, are eligible 
for the rehabilitation assistance available to sick units in the small scale industries 
(SSI) sector, as per the guidelines of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). These 
measures include, inter-alia: 
(i) Waiver of penal interest on cash credit and term loan from the year the 
unit started making cash losses. 
(ii) Unpaid interest on cash credit and term loan should be segregated from 
the total liability and the former amount treated as a separate interest-free loan. 
(iii) Reduced rate of interest (reduction of upto 3 per cent for tiny units and of 
upto 2 per cent for SSI units) should be charged on unpaid term loans. 
(iv)Additional working capital loan should be given at a rate of interest not 
exceeding the prime lending rate.

Statement-ll 
Criteria for upgrading/opening Departmental Sub Post Offices 
(a) In Rural Areas: 
The minimum work load of the Extra Departmental Branch Post Office, 
proposed to be upgraded, should be five hours per day. The permissible limit of 
annual loss is Rs. 2400/- in Normal Rural areas and Rs. 4800/- in Tribal and 
Hilly areas. 
It is further to be ensured that a result of the opening of a new post office, 
the loss in respect of the parent post office does not increase beyond the 
permissible limit nor is its income reduced below the minimum prescribed. 
(b) In Urban Areas: 
In Urban areas, the post office should initially be self-supporting and, at the 
time of the first annual review, it should show a 5% profit to be eligible for 
further retention. 
31 

RAJYA SABHA [9 December, 2004] 
The minimum distance between two post offices should be 1.5 Kms in cities with a 
population of 20 lakhs and above, and 2 Kms in other Urban Areas. No two delivery offices, 
however, should be closer than 5 Kms from each other. 
Heads of Circles have powers to relax the distance condition in 10% of the cases. 
A Delivery Post Office in Urban Areas should have a minimum of 7 Postmen's 
beats.

New coal companies 
*127. SHRI PYARIMOHAN MOHAPATRA: Will the Minister of COAL 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the norms in terms of production and profits for establishment of new 
coal companies and the names of companies which do not satisfy the norms; 
(b) whether Talcher Division of Mahanadi Coalfields Limited can be 
constituted into a separate company on the basis of its production, profits and 
potential; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF COAL (SHRI SHIBU SOREN): (a) No norms have 
been laid down for establishment of new coal companies. However, an Expert 
Committee on Public Sector Undertakings under the Chairmanship of Mr. Md. 
Fazal, the then Member, Planning Commission, submitted a Report in 
November, 1980 (Fazal Committee Report) which laid down that for creating a 
separate coal company, the optimal production that should be handled and 
managed by a viable coal company should be in the region of approx. 20 million 
tonnes annually. After 1980, there have been enormous technological changes in 
the mining industry and heavy earth moving machinery is getting bigger and 
bigger in size. There are single mines producing even 30-40 million tonnes 
abroad per annum. The 20 million tonnes figure, therefore, needs to be 
revisited. 
Administrative convenience and opening of new areas are some of the factors 
that are taken into consideration for opening up of new coal companies. On 
this basis in the past SECL, NCL and MCL coal companies were created. But now 
international climate has changed and experience shows that big companies can 
organize business in a more efficient and organized way and can perform better in 
comparison to smaller companies in view of better technology, trained man-
power, better economics of production and better bargaining power in purchase of 
equipment and other items. All coal producing subsidiary companies of Coal 
India Limited produce more than 20 million tonnes of coal annually. 
(b) and (c) Talcher Division of Mahanadi Coalfields Ltd. (MCL), produced 42.06 
million tonnes ofcoal in 2003-04. MCL was formed in 1992 by carving out part of 
the coalfields under South Eastern Coalfields Ltd. (SECL) that

fell in the territory of Orissa State. No operational or administrative 
constraints are being experienced by MCL in the management and 
development of coal mines in the Talcher area. Since MCL has been formed only in 
1992 looking to the fast growth potential of the lb Valley and Talcher area and 
economic, administrative and operational conveniences and other factors, creation 
of a new coal company for the Talcher Coalfields is not considered necessary 
at present.

694. SHRI RAJ KUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of AGRO AND RURAL 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have dissolved the Khadi and Village 
Industries Commission on 14th October, 2004 and made some stop gap 
arrangements before its restructuring; 
54 

[9 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the details thereof alongwith the reasons for acting in haste in this 
regard; 
(c) whether it was not considered appropriate to work out to revamp the 
Commission to make it professionally competent rather than dissolving it; and 
(d) if not, the benefit expected to be achieved for KVIC, promoted 
manufacturing units and for consumers by such a decision? 
THE MINISTER OF AGROAND RURAL INDUSTRIES (SHRI MAHABIR 
PRASAD): (a) and (b) In the National Common Minimum Programme, the 
Government has declared to revamp  the Khadi and Village Industries 
Commission (KVIC). This has been necessitated mainly because of the steep 
decline in employment in the Khadi sector and nearly stagnant sales of Khadi 
over the years, the need to take effective measures to introduce modern 
management practices in the KVIC and make the Khadi products competitive in 
the globalised economy and to enable the Government to generate more 
employment opportunities in the rural areas through the schemes, projects and 
other activities of the KVIC. 
As one of the steps towards this objective, the Government has dissolved the 
Commission with effect from 14 October, 2004 in exercise of its powers under 
section 25(1) of the KVIC Act, 1956? Subsequent to the dissolution of the 
Commission, an authority Called Commissioner for Khadi and Village Industries 
has been established as an interim meas ure, to carry on the functions of the 
KVIC. The Commissioner for Khadi and Village Industries has been authorized 
to exercise the powers of the Commiss ion on the date of its dissolution, 
including execution of the programmes and policies being implemented by the 
dissolved Commission. 
By an order dated 1 December, 2004, the Government has also set up a ten-
Member Expert Committee with the terms of reference to, inter alia, review the 
existing structure, functioning and performance of the KVIC since its 
inception as well as the provisions of  the Khadi and Village Industries 
Commission Act, 1956, Rules thereunder, etc., and recommend restructuring, 
along with modifications, if any, in these statutes. 
The dissolution of the Commission is a well-considered decision of the 
Government and there is no question of acting in haste. 
(c) The Expert Committee (EC) has been mandated to go into all aspects of the 
functioning and performance of the KVIC since its inception. Such a thorough 
review would not have been possible with the statutory nominated

Inquiry to fix accountability on errant operators 
717. SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Will the Minister of COMMUNICATIONS 
AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a grey market has emerged since the 
interconnect usage charge regime of Government has been established in May, 
2003 to deny BSNL Rs. 4.25 per international call; 
(b) whether Government have conducted any inquiry to fix accountability on 
errant operators who are fleecing the BSNL and thereby restricting expansion 
of the network in rural and backward areas; and 
(c) if so, the findings thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMUNICATIONS 
AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. SHAKEEL AHMAD): (a) No, 
Sir. Grey Market exists much before May, 2003. The first case was detected in 1998. 
(b) Yes, Sir. The Government has conducted a detailed inquiry and has found 
that one of the errant operators M/s Reliance Infocom Limited was routing 
incoming international calls with domestic CLI (Calling Line Identification) 
in trunk groups meant for domestic calls in violation of the License Agreement 
of Government of India, as well as Interconnect Agreeement with BSNL. 
(c) M/s Reliance Infocom was found routing incoming international calls with 
domestic CLI in trunk groups meant for domestic calls, i.e. M/s Reliance has brought 
incoming international calls to India and handed over to BSNL as domestic calls 
after changing the calling line identification of these calls. M/s Reliance have 
neither intimated nor paid charges to BSNL as applicable for incoming 
international calls. Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) in its IUC 
(Interconnection Usage Charge) Regulation had prescribed that applicable 
Access Deficit Charge (ADC) for incoming international calls is Rs. 4.25 per 
minute and for incoming domestic calls originated from fixed networks the 
applicable ADC is NIL. M/s RIL handed over such calls to BSNL as if such calls 
had originated in India from fixed networks of M/s RIL and, therefore, applicable 
ADC. This not only resulted in bypass of ADC of BSNL but also was violative of 
security instructions of Government. This is also violative of the terms and 
conditions of license 
103 

RAJYA SABHA [9 December, 2004] 
granted to them as they tempered with the CLI of the calling party. And for violation of 
license agreement a notice for imposing penalty of Rs. 150 crones have been issued by 
DoT to M/s Reliance on 24.11.2004. For this violation as per the IUC agreement, BSNL has 
asked M/s Reliance Infocom Limited to pay Rs. 182 crore on 29th October, 2004. However, 
M/s Reliance Infocom Limited appealed against this before the Hon'ble High Court. BSNL had 
filed an SLP(C) in the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India on 22nd November, 2004 to grant 
stay against the interim order dated 5th November, 2004 of the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi. 
The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in its order dated 3rd December, 2004 has directed M/s 
RIL to make full payment as claimed by BSNL vide its letter dated 29th October, 2004 i.e. 
sum of Rs. 182.7 crores within a period of 4 weeks and subject to this payment by M/s RIL 
there shall be stay on the disconnection of its POIs by BSNL. The Hon'ble Supreme Court 
of India has also directed M/s RIL to file an affidavit that it is not changing the CLI of the 
international calls. While the total dues pending on M/s Reliance Infocom Limited as 
on 5.11.04 was Rs. 257 crore, M/s Reliance Infocom Limited has only paid approximately 
Rs. 100 crore so far. Similarly, MTNL has made a claim of Rs. 341.27 crores against M/s 
Reliance Infocom Limited and Reliance Infocom Limited has paid Rs. 66.76 
crores to MTNL.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI RAO INDERJIT SINGH): (a) to (c) An agreement has been reached 
between what is now being termed as the 'Group of Four Aspirants'— Brazil, 
India, Germany and Japan—that these countries are legitimate candidates for 
permanent membership in an expanded Security Council and will support each 
other's candidature. They also agreed th at Africa must also be represented in 
the permanent membership of  Security Council. A su mmit of the leaders of 
these four countries was held on September 21, 2004 in New York which was 
attended by Hon'ble Prime Minister of India, President of Brazil, Prime Minister 
of Japan and Deputy Chancellor of Germany. The summit was a significant 
statement of intent by these four countries to participate in the UN reform 
process on the basis of a mutual understanding to support each other. 
Subsequently, the Foreign Ministers of these four countries held a meeting in 
New York on 24 September, 2004 to plan the future work to realize the 
objective. 
(d) Some countries, including Pakistan, are known to be opposing the 
expansion of the UN Security Council in the permanent category. 
(e) Decisions on reforms are to be considered by the entire membership of the 
UN and accodingly views of any country have to be seen in this perspective. 
India believes that the reform and restru cturing exercise is important and that 
by an objective criteria, India's case is credible and strong. There is growing 
momentum in support of India's candidature for permanent membership.

Policy to deal with hostage crisis 
742. SHRI AMAR SINGH: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have not evolved any official policy 
on how to deal with the hostage situations despite the fact that a 
131 

RAJYA SABHA [9 December, 2004] 
number of such unfortunate incidents have taken place several times during the past; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether Government propose to evolve any such policy; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and by when? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI E. 
AHAMMED): (a) to (d) It is the policy of the Government of India not to compromise 
with terrorist groups or elements. However, while adhering to this principle, the objective 
of the Government is to ensure the safety and well-being of all its citizens, whether in India or 
abroad. In case of hostage-taking, Government makes all efforts possible to secure the 
early and safe release of its nationals. In order to deal with hostage situations, the 
Government have an institutionalized mechanism in place. There is a Crisis Management 
Group which is set up immediately and is tasked with the constant monitoring and handling 
of the situation in close consultation with concerned agencies, our diplomatic missions 
abroad and with foreign governments. The Cabinet Secretary also holds a parallel set of inter-
ministerial meetings, as required, to take appropriate decision. The Cabinet Committee on 
Political Affairs may also meet, as necessary, to review the situation and take appropriate 
decisions. This mechanism remains in force until the crisis ends. It needs to be pointed 
out that no two hostage situations are entirely similar and different responses may be 
required depending upon specific circumstances to reach the objectives of Government 
policy.

Indo-Pak discussions 
†750. SHRI R.S. GAVAI: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) the details of the discussions taken place during last three years between India 
Pakistan; and 
(b) the subjects that would come for discussion in future? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI E. 
AHAMMED): (a) and (b) Following the terrorist attack on Parliament on December 
13, 2001, India had taken a number of steps, including the recall of the High Commissioner, 
termination of Delhi-Lahore bus service, Samjhauta Express, air links, and reduction 
in size of respective High Commissions. India also impressed upon Pakistan the need to 
put an end to cross border infiltration and terrorism, and to dismantle the infrastructure of support 
to terrorism in Pakistan on a permanent basis. 
Later, after India extended the hand of friendship to Pakistan in April 2003, and 
based on the commitment given by President Musharraf on January 6,2004 not to permit 
any territory under Pakistan's control to be used to support terrorism in any manner, the 
Composite Dialogue was resumed. Steps were taken to normalize diplomatic and other links. 
Within the framework of the Composite Dialogue, discussions were held on the subjects of 
Peace and Security including CBMs, Jammu and Kashmir, Siachen, Sir Creek, Tulbul 
Navigation Project, Terrorism and Drug Trafficking, Economic and Commercial 
Cooperation, and Promotion of Friendly Exchanges in Various Fields. India made a 
large number of proposals for confidence building, interaction and cooperation. 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
138 

[9 Decernber, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
A number of technical meeting on various subjects were also held, including on 
opening new routes and communication links, and between BSF and Pakistan Rangers, and 
Narcotics control authorities on the issues related to border management, and combating 
the menace of drug trafficking and smuggling. 
The Foreign Ministers of India and Pakistan met in New Delhi on September 5-
6,2004 to review overall progress in the Composite Dialogue. They exchange views on 
carrying the process forward in an atmosphere free from terrorism and violence. The two 
Ministers agreed to a number of technical level meetings on various subjects, including expert 
level meetings on Conventional and Nuclear CBMs, inter alia, to discuss the draft 
agreement on advance notification of missile tests; meeting between Indian Border Security 
Force (BSF) and Pakistan Rangers; meeting between railway authorites on the Munnabao-
Khokhrapar rail link; meeting between Narcotics Control Authorities, including for finalisation 
of an MOU; meeting between the Indian Coast Guards and the Pakistan Maritime 
Security Agency to, inter alia, discuss the Memoranum of Understanding for 
establishing communication link between them; and meeting on all issues related to 
commencement of a bus service between Srinagar and Muzaffarabad. They also 
agreed to the establishment of a Committee of Experts to consider issues related to trade; a 
Joint Survey of the boundary pillars in the horizontal segment of the international 
boundary in the Sir Creek area; addition of a new category of Tourist Visa in the visa 
regime between the two countries, and to promote group tourism; set up a 
mechanism to deal with the issue of civilian prisoners and firshermen, effectively and 
speedily; undertake further measures for facilitation of visits to religious shrines, and upkeep 
of historical sites; implement the outcome of the August 2004 meeting of Defence 
Secretaries; and enhanced interaction and exchanges among the respective Foreign Offices, 
including study tours of young diplomats/probationers to each other's country. 
They, inter alia, agreed to continue with the serious and sustained dialogue, and 
reiterated the confidence that the Composite Dialogue will lead to peaceful settlement of all 
bilateral issues to the satisfaction of both sides. 
The prcoess has been taken forward through high level meetings and visits, including the 
meeting between Prime Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh and President Musharraf in New 
York on September 24,2004 and the visit

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF MINES (DR DASARI 
NARAYANA RAO): (a) As per the National Mineral Policy (NMP), 1993, the non-fuel 
and non-atomic mineral sector has been thrown open for private investment including 
Foreign Direct Investment 
(b) to (e) For non-fuel and non-atomic minerals, the above mentioned National Mineral

the availability of the mineral and economic viability of their exploration and 
exploitation, whenever any major changes are made in the said Act or Rules, generally all 
stakeholders including State Governments are consulted in the matter.

803. SHRI NANDI YELLAIAH: Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND

(a) the details of progress made so far by the Department of Science and 
Technology under the National Jai Vigyan Science and Technology Mission; 
(b) the details of progress made on new generation of vaccines specially with 
regards to HIV/AIDS, which has become a great menace to our Nation and the

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) Department of Science and 
Technology is implementing four Jai Vigyan National Science and 
Technology Missions. The progress is as follows: 
i. Mission for Visually Impaired 
A LPG stove has been successfully designed and demonstrated which helps 
the blind towards understanding the position of hands in the 3D space in 
relation to the burner and knob position. It has a provision for auto ignition of 
burners. 
A manually operated machine has been developed for printing different types 
of maps for visually impaired. Semi-automatic screen printing machine is being 
developed in order to improve the quality of maps and printing in larger formats. 
199 

RAJYA SABHA [9 December, 2004] 
ii. Mission for Natural Hazard Mitigation in Himalaya 
Seismic observatories have been installed and commissioned at five locations in North-
Eastern India. A multicomponent programme to monitor geomagnetic, geoelectrical and 
very low frequency (VLF) electromagnetic emissions to isolate and understand the nature 
of precursory signals of earthquakes in the Himalaya has been initiated. Microzonation 
map of landslide affected area between Banderdeva and Gohpur in Arunachal Pradesh 
has been prepared. 
iii. Area Development Mission for Andaman & Nicobar Islands 
A Plasma Pyrolysis Plant based on indigenous technology has been set up for disposal 
of plastic waste at Port Blair. Inventory of medicinal plants with special reference to 
plants used by the indigenous tribes and settlers has been completed. Training 
programmes on fish and prawn aquaculture and solid waste management through 
vermiculture techniques have been conducted for skill development of the beneficiaries of the 
island. 
iv. Jai Vigyan Swasthya Project for Rural Areas 
Software has been developed and hardware has been procured. The Core Centre 
(Hospital) has started functioning at Vijayawada. Connectivity of the Core Centre with 
Regional Diagnositc Centres (RDCs) and General Practitioners (GPs) has been 
established. 
(b) the Department of Bio-technology is supporting research and development 
efforts towards development of new generation vaccines for diseases like Cholera, 
Rabies, Tuberculosis, Malaria, Japanese Encephalitis and HIV/AIDS under the 
National Jai Vigyan Science and Technology Mission. The details of progress are as 
follows: 
i. Cholera: 
An indigenous recombinant oral vaccine based on VA 1.3 strain on V. cholerae has 
been developed and extended Phase-l/Phase-lla clinical trial have been undertaken. A new 
vaccine strain VA 1.4 without the ampicilin marker has been prepared and is undergoing 
toxicological studies. 
200 

[9 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
ii. Tuberculosis: 
Recombinant forms of two promising candidate T-cell antigens of M. 
tuberculosis i.e. ARR65, ARR213 are being tested for immune response. 
Recombinant approach for the development of novel candidate vaccine/s against 
tuberculosis is being studied by expressing six antigens of M. tuberculosis 
using different vectors and E. co//expression system. 
iii. Rabies: 
The world's first Combination Rabies Vaccine consisting of DNA vaccine and a 
low dose of inactivated cell-cultured Rabi es vaccine for control of Rabies in 
dogs has been developed. The vaccine was found to confer 100 percent protection 
in experimental animals. The Indian Immunologicals Ltd., Hyderabad, will 
commercialize this vaccine after successful completion of the multicentric animal 
trials and approval by the regulatory authorities.

been developed, the technology has been transferred to Industry for further 
testing and commercialization.

Good Laboratory Practices (GLP) grade vaccine production facility has been 
established at the International Centre for Genetic Engineering and Bio-
technology (ICGEB), New Delhi. Methods  have been developed to express 
recombinant Plasmodium falciparum Merozoite Surface Protein (PfMSP19) 
and the technology is being scaled up by Industry. Clinical trials sites are 
being developed. 
vi. HIV 
A prototype Candidate Vaccine for the HIV-I Subtype 'C has been 
developed based on plas mid DNA and Modified Vaccinia Ankara (MVA) 
approaches. The prototype HIV-I Vaccine candidate induces a robust and broad 
based clade-specific and cross-clade immune response in immunized monkeys and is 
now ready for preclinical toxicological studies. Negotiations

with an Indian industry are also in progress for Good Manufacturing Practices 
grade production of vaccinogens; and to coduct human clinical trials.

logistic support towards launching major multicentric and interactive R&D 
projects for development of diagnostic test systems, molecular typing of 
HIV/AIDS isolates, immunological and vi rological responses in normal and 
infected human subjects, vaccine delivery systems and establishment of a virus 
bank, which have paved the way towards design and development of appropriate 
vaccine candidates in this country. New programmes have been initiated for 
identification and characterization of HIV receptors on spermatozoa, factors

816. SHRI S.M. LALJAN BASHA: Will the Minister of SHIPPING, ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the fact that the Container Port at Mumbai is totally 
congested and has become inefficient; 
212 

[9 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) the reasons for the inefficient operation of this Container Port at the JNPT; 
(c) whether proper planning has not been done; 
(d) the steps proposed to suggest immediate measures to reduce the congestion 
presently prevailing at JNPT; 
(e) whether Government are aware of the huge losses being suffered by trade and 
industry; and 
(f) the steps proposed to review the capacity of the management at this Port? 
THE MINISTER OF SHIPPING, ROAD TRANSPORT AND 
HIGHWAYS (SHRI T.R. BAALU): (a) to.(f) Mumbai Port and Jawaharlai Nehru Port 
(JNPT) are two ports located in Mumbai. So far as Mumbai Port is concerned, there 
has not been any problem of congestion. However, container terminals located at 
Jawaharlai Nehru Port, namely, Jawaharlai Nehru Container Terminal (JNPCT) and 
Nhava Sheva International Container Terminal (NSICT) have been witnessing 
congestion particularly during the months of September and October, 2004. The 
problem came up mainly because of increased volume of traffic, which created a lot 
of strain on the existing infrastructure at JNPT. The congestion is further 
attributable to floods in the monsoon season, which badly affected the operations of 
Container Corporation of India (CONCOR) and as a result Inland Container Depot (ICD) 
bound containers could not be lifted. Further, delay in taking delivery of import 
consignments by the consignees or agents from the Container Freight Stations (CFS), 
poor road conditions in Dronagiri Node connecting various CFSs with JNPT and 
road congestion resulting due to inadequate parking facilities and waiting of 
container carrying Tractor-Trailors on JNPT roads for Customs documentation 
added to the complexity of the situation. It is correct that because of congestion, 
the Exim-Trade experienced difficulties in smooth movement of 
213 

RAJYA SABHA [9 December, 2004] 
containers through Jawaharlal Nehru Port during the period of congestion. 
However, volume of container traffic during the current year, despite 
congestion, has gone up as reflected from the following data:—

with concerned departments, agenci es and trade and commerce. These 
discussions culminated into initiation of numerous measures aimed at 
immediate easing of the congestion at JNPT as also for long-term solutions 
besides the realization that the actual traffic allowed should be related to the 
capacity of terminal(s). Some of the important decisions are as under:— 
* As an emergency measure the NSICT was permitted by Customs to 
remove the container from, container terminals to CWC, Kalamboli, 
CWC, Sheva, CWC, Distripark and DRT CONCOR en-block. 
* CBEC (Central Board of Excise & Customs) has allowed waiver of 
bank guarantee for the period of three months with effect from 
1.11.2004, for transshipment of containers by road all the shipping lines 
registered with the Jawaharlal Nehru Customs House (JNCH). 
* Import of heavy metal scrap containers through JNPT/NSICT has been 
banned from 15 September, 2004 to 15th January, 2005. 
* JNPT added for more reach stackers during the year in addition to 11 
existing.

Problems of SSIs 
†827. SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: 
SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH MAJITHA: 
Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have considered to solve the problems to be faced by small 
scale industries of the country during the mid-term review of Tenth Five Year Plan; 
(b) if so, the major problems of small scale industries of the country; 
(c) whether there is any role of Government to solve these problems; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (SHRI MAHABIR PRASAD): 
(a) to (d) The Government is aware of the problems faced by the Small Scale Industries (SSI) 
sector. Inadequate and delayed credit is one of the major problems of the small scale industries. 
Similarly, obsolete technology, inadequate infrastructure, marketing constraints and fiscal anomalies 
are some of the other problems faced by the SSI sector as a whole. 
The Government continues to lay emphasis on solving the problems faced by the SSI 
sector, various measures, which seek to facilitate better availability of credit, technology 
upgradation and infrastructure and ease the marketing constraints, have been taken for 
imparting more vitality and growth impetus to this sector. 
These measures include the following plan schemes:— 
(1) Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme for Small Industries:—This scheme was launched 
with the objective of making credit available to SSI units, particularly tiny units, for 
loans upto Rs. 25 lakh without collateral/third party guarantees. The scheme covers 
collateral-free credit facility (both term loan and/or working capital) by eligible lending 
institutions, to new and existing SSI units, including information technology and 
software industries of the small scale sector, upto Rs. 25 lakh (per borrowing unit). With 
effect from September 1,2003, new and existing Small Scale Service and Business (industry 
related) Enterprises (SSSBEs) have also been 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
226 

[9 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
made eligible for coverage under the scheme. The guarantee cover is upto 75% of 
the credit, subject to a maximum guarantee limit of Rs. 18.75 lakh. 
(2) Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme (CLCSS):—This scheme was 
launched in 2000, to encourage SSI units to adopt the latest technology and improve 
the quality of their products. Under this scheme, 12 per cent capital subsidy is 
admissible on loans advanced by th e scheduled commercial banks/State 
Finance Corporations, upto a maximum loan amount of Rs. 40 lakh, to the SSI 
units for induction of well established/ improved technologies. 
(3) ISO 9000 Certification Reimbursement Scheme:—Government 
launched this incentive scheme for technology upgradation, quality 
improvement and environment managment of small scale industries, in order to 
enhance their competitiveness. The scheme provides incentive to the small scale 
units, which have acquired ISO 9000/14001 certifications. The scheme envisages 
reimbursement of charges for acquiring ISO 9000 and/or IS014001 certification to 
the extent of 75 per cent of the expenditure, subject to a maximum of Rs. 75,000 in 
total, per unit. 
(4) Small Industry Cluster Development Programme:—This programme aims 
at undertaking studies for assessing technology status/technology needs of 
identified clusters of traditional skill-based enterprises and fac ilitating 
contact/need-based research, to adapt the available technology to the specific 
needs of the end users and to promote and facilitate the delivery assimilation 
and diffusion of the identified technology from its producers, to the recipient 
users/clusters of small enterprises. 
(5) Integrated Infrastructural Develo pment (llD) Scheme:—This scheme 
provides essential infrastructural facilities at various locations in the country, for 
setting up of SSI and tiny units. The thrust of the scheme is to make developed 
sites available with infrastructur e facilities like power, water, 
telecommunications, drainage, pollution control facilities, roads, banks, raw 
material depots, storage and marketing outlets, etc. Another important objective of 
the scheme is to upgrade/strengthen the infrastructure facilities in the existing/old 
industrial estates. Under this scheme, the project cost to establish an IID Centre 
has a normative ceiling of Rs. 5 crore (excluding cost of land), the Central 
Government provides grant of 40 per cent subject to a maximum of Rs. 2 crore per 
IID Centre in general and of 80 per cent, subject to a maximum of Rs. 4 crore per 
IID Centre in the North Eastern 
227 

RAJYA SABHA [9 December, 2004] 
Region (including Sikkim), Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttaranchal. 
This remaining amount could be a loan from the Small Industries Development Bank 
of India/Banks/Financial Institutions or from the State Government concerned. 
(6) Marketing Assistance and Export Promotion Scheme:—This scheme, designed to 
facilitate export by the SSI sector, extends a number of incentives and facilities to small 
scale exporters, viz., participation in the international trade fairs/exhibitions, imparting 
training on packaging for exports and market development assistance for individual 
participation, in the fairs abroad. Under this scheme, financial assistance is also given to 
small scale units for adoption of-bar coding registration with European Article 
Numbering (EAN) India.

839. SHRI TARIQ ANWAR: Will the Minister of STATISTICS AND 
PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that MPLADS funds have not been utilised by the several 
States during the last two years; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor;

funds; and

PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION (SHRI OSCAR FERNANDES): (a) All States

preparation of estimates by the concerned agencies; (iii) delay in issue of financial sanction

direction to all concerned. The officers of the Ministry of Statistics and Programme 
Implementation will take up State-wise review at State Headquarters to expedite the 
implementation of the Scheme. The software launched on 30.11.2004 for monitoring of 
MPLADS works will be operationalised in all the districts.

SHRI FALI S. NARIMAN: Sir, I thought that I would speak when the Opposition are 
there because it is not much fun speaking to the converted. Therefore, I would have preferred it 
but, unfortunately,'because of certain circumstances, it is not possible. 
My learned, distinguished friend, and, colleague Mr. Jaitley spoke at the end about 
when history comes to be written, and, he warned the Home Minister that when history 
comes to be written, it will be very much against the proponents of this Bill. Sir, when the 
history of this period comes to be written about anything at all, we will all be dead and I 
don't think that this attention about history comes to be written has anything except a 
euphoric effect. I recall General de Gaulle saying once that we cannot confuse the breezes 
of fashion with the winds of history. We don't know what the winds of history may say, but I will 
deal with the breezes of fashion, not with any political slant but strictly as a nominated 
Member, and, please don't forgtet a Member nominated by the party of which Mr. 
Jaitley was the Minister. 
Sir, there is always much politics about POTA, and, there always has been much politics 
about POTA. I am not going to speak about the politics of POTA Two principal parties have been 
polarised, on POTA which became a political issue ever since many of us including myself 
voted against it in the year 2002, both in this House, and, in the joint session of the two 
Houses. Sir, if POTA had been totally repealed, I would have been the first to oppose it, both 
because an anti-terrorist law is required, and, it is 
318 

[9 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA  
mandated under the UN Security Resolution But, this Bill, almost word for word, draws 
upon the provisions of POTA, and, removes the harshness of the procedural provisions, not the 
substantive provisions which I hope to demonstrate. Does it remove its teeth? The answer is 
'no'. I believe it does not, and, that is why, I support it. In fact, Sir, if there was such a thing as 
a copyright in a statute, this would have been a Bill copyrighted by the NDA, and the 
present Government would have been the guilty of a breach of copyright for copying the 
provision of POTA. Sir, there is an idea which is prevalent amongst many people, and, I regret 
to say, wrongly prevalent, both in this House as well as outside. That only a harsh law 
contain terrorism. Sir, if you look at Section 3 of the old Act and Clause 15 of the Bill, 
defining terrorist act and Persuading Punishment. You will find that the provisions are 
identical. In fact, there is one thing more. The punishment--that is I am talking now of the 
substantive isw-for the terrorist act is identical; it is the same. There is no difference in the 
punishment. Therefore, to say that the present Bill is not a harsh substantive law, would 
be erroneous. Yes, procedurally, there are points which I wish to mention. You can 
introduce the harshest law on terrorism, but you will never effectively counter it unless 
there is a detailed method of investigation and a proper marshalling of evidence in a court of 
law, because a court of law requires not suspicion, but evidence. Therefore, the key detection for 
cases of terrorism for the prosecuting agency is to marshal the evidence, such evidence as 
they gather. And, in fact, I have always believed, and if the Home Minister does not mind my 
saying so, that there are better safeguards in our preventive detention Law than in any other law 
for apprehending the terrorist. In fact, the ancient, almost now ancient, National Security Act is 
still in force, and the reason why a preventive detention law is more appropriate for a 
terrorist that a trial law is simply because, in respect of a terrorist activity, howsoever widely-
defined, there is an inherent difficulty in its being established against a person accused in a 
court of law. Even, under the provisions of POTA, the previous Governments have found it 
extraordinarily difficult and the State Governments have found it extraordinary 
difficult to convict terrorists, to arrest them, to detain them, to Jail them. Then, you mix up 
the good with the bad. A large number of people were taken in, some people were 
detained for very long periods and ultimately they were found to be innocent of the offence, or, 
not guility, at least, of the offence. I would suggest to the hon. Home Minister, in 
consultation with the Law Minister, also to take into account and try to 
319 

RAJYA SABHA [9 December, 2 004] 
revive this so-called 'dead' National Security Act and invoke some of its 
provisions for the detention of terrorists for which purpose, if an appropriate Bill is 
necessary, it may come in the next session. 
If you look elsewhere, Sir, you will find there was a stormy debate in the British 
Parliament on their Terrorism and Crime Act which was enacted in February, 
2002, and it provides not for prosecution or trial like POTO or POTA, but for 
indefinite detention for a period, with out charge, of non-British national, 
reasonably suspected by the Home Secretary to be involved in terrorist acts. It is now 
proposed to extend it even to the British nationals as well. And, people have forgotten 
what happened two years ago. You will recall that President Musharraf tried to 
ridicule us before the internatipnal fora, when confronted with the abduction and 
murder of the Wall Street journal reporter, Daniel P earl, the American 
correspondent. The man who is supposed to have murdered him was Omar 
Sheikh. He was the same Omar Sheikh who was detained in Jammu and Kashmir 
for nearly 5 years t ill he was released in exchange for passengers held as 
hostages in Kandahar on IC-814. Why? Simply because if he was tried, the 
evidence produced in court would not have justified the conviction. There was only a 
grave suspicion, the gravest possible suspicion of his involvement in terrorist act, but 
no proof that would stand up in a court of law. You will recall that Pervez 
Musharraf ridiculed us and said why did not the Indian Government prosecute and 
bring Omar Sheikh to trial for 5 long years. The General knew the answer, but 
he would not say it and, the answer is that the terrorist activity is in the realm of 
grave suspicion, seldom in the range of proof. The even-handedness of State 
Governments in administering POTA could not be ensured because of the harsh 
procedural.provisions. And, despite the setting up of a Review Committee, you 
will all recall, how the then Home Minister came here one year after POTA and 
agreed with the House that it was being misused by various States. In fact, he 
himself propounded an amendment to the review provision, which provided for a 
High Court judge to go into individal cases notwithstanding a court going into it. It 
is no longer there in the law, because it is not necessary now. But it is important to 
know that the Government of the day, at that point of time, itself felt the need for 
some machinery to alleviate the rigors of this very, very harsh procedural law. 
Recently, some Members and people outside have asked me as to how this 
amending Bill is different. Are we 'better off? Or are we 'worse off? And 
320 

[9 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA  
my submission, after reading it and comparing the provisions, is that we are 'better off. By 'we' I 
mean 'the innocent citizens of India'. If terrorists are not 'better off, we are not concerned. Of 
course, they do not have to be better off". Are they 'better off? The former Minister said that they 
were "better off", they would be smiling; and they would be laughing and things of that sort The 
former Minister said that they would be laughing and they would be rejoicing and so on. I do 
not believe that. Why? Because the very same provisions, which they enacted in POTA, have 
been reproduced in the present Bill. All the substantive provisions, except the procedural provisions 
to which I will come in a moment, Sir, if you do not mind, are there. 
First, in POTA, 2002, the Criminal Procedure Code was amended to provide for the 
extended period of fetention without trial. The police could do nothing for the six months, 
whereas the maximum period under Criminal Procedure Code is 90 days, really speaking 24 
hours, or one month, or at the most three months under various magistrates' orders. Now, 
this is absent and done away with by the current Bill. That is number one. 
Second, in criminal law, the ordinary principle for all undertrials is, as my friend rightly 
said, "bail not jail", as Justice Krishna Iyer used to put it. And the principle was really 
constricted by the provisions, of POTA and if you look at the sub-sections 6, 7, and 8 of 
Section 49 of POTA, you will know. Why these provisions are not in the new Bill. They 
were the most obnoxious provisions of POTA, and capable, of being used and which 
were used, misused and abused by many, many agencies of various State Governments. No 
person accused of an offence under POTA was to be released on bail, unless the court gave 
the public prosecutor an opportunity of being heard, and until the court was satisfied that there 
were groudns for believing that the accused was not guilty of committing the offence. Just 
imagine, anybody would be picked up, and the accussed would have to prove that he was 
innocent in order to get bail, which is an impossible situation! He could never get it, and 
therefore, he would be incarcerated for a minimum period of 180 days. And if the police 
could not make a charge, he would then be released, and there was no appreciated bail for 
one full year after detention. 
Many members have said that there should be very, very stringent provisions for 
bail. But, Sir, I regret to say, with these methods of interceptions and communications, 
it is easy to frame any body. The other
